Andrewes House.name: Andrewes House
Andrewes House.story: Vicar of St Giles Cripplegate from 1589 (arranged by Walsingham); said to speak fifteen languages.
Andrewes House.completed_note: July or November 1969 depending on source; Phase III, John Laing; known as Block VIII until completed.
Andrewes House.types_note: 13 flat types, 2- to 4-room; regular flats, penthouses, and two storeys of garden (sub-podium) flats. Only block whose garden flats have individual gardens/patios (facing Fore Street, behind a high wall).
Andrewes House.views: Front-to-back (east-west) block along the south side of the lake. Living rooms face south over Fore Street; bedrooms face north over the lake. Sits between Gilbert House and Willoughby House.
Andrewes House.features: Penthouses with barrel-vaulted roofs; sub-podium garden flats with private gardens; tenants stores and car park at 03 level.
Andrewes House.entrance: Entrances on Andrewes Highwalk at podium level; street access from Fore Street and Wood Street via lift/stair 49 (next to the bar/restaurant). Nearest Tube not stated on source.

listing.note: Single list entry for the whole Barbican complex (listed 5 Sep 2001); blocks are not separately listed.

Ben Jonson House.name: Ben Jonson House
Ben Jonson House.story: Taken out of school to lay bricks like his stepfather, he joined the army in Flanders and killed a Spanish soldier in single combat before taking up the theatre.
Ben Jonson House.types_note: Mostly maisonettes with internal stairs (corridors on levels 2, 3 and 5 only), plus two- and three-storey penthouses.
Ben Jonson House.views: Longest terrace block in the estate, north podium, spans Golden Lane. North side looks over the Golden Lane Estate and a school playground; south side faces Frobisher Crescent, Defoe House and the Barbican Centre.
Ben Jonson House.features: Longest block; passes over Golden Lane; paired balconies on levels 2, 3 and 5; dolphin fountain at the front on Ben Jonson Place; round-arched glazed roof-level rooms.
Ben Jonson House.entrance: Lift 62 (west end) to Bridgewater Street; lift 63 (centre) to Beech Street; lift 64 (east end) to Whitecross Street. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

listing.note: Single list entry for the whole Barbican complex (listed 5 Sep 2001); blocks are not separately listed.

Breton House.name: Breton House
Breton House.story: Son of a rich merchant of Red Cross Street (now buried under the estate); his stepfather was the poet George Gascoigne.
Breton House.types_note: Studios (types F1A, F2A) and one-bedroom penthouse maisonettes (type P2A).
Breton House.views: North boundary of the estate, at right angles to the middle of Ben Jonson House. East flats overlook Whitecross Street; west flats overlook Cripplegate Library and Golden Lane. Mirror image of John Trundle Court.
Breton House.features: Rooftop penthouses with round-arched glazed form; raised mezzanine entrances; sub-podium level has no flats.
Breton House.entrance: Raised entrances up external stairs to lobbies serving clusters of five flats; lifts 65-67; fire exit to Golden Lane. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

listing.note: Single list entry for the whole Barbican complex (listed 5 Sep 2001); blocks are not separately listed.

Bryer Court.name: Bryer Court
Bryer Court.named_after: W. Bryer & Sons, gold refiners and assayers, who occupied 53-54 Barbican on the site
Bryer Court.story: A frieze of the gold-refining process saved from their building is on the wall in White Lyon Court, facing Blake Tower.
Bryer Court.types_note: All studio flats (virtually identical); narrowest block on the estate.
Bryer Court.views: North-south block on the north podium; all flats face west, single aspect (Murray House built 1956 stands directly behind). Its own small lake with fountains in Beech Gardens at the front.
Bryer Court.features: Narrowest block; small pool with fountains; access gallery at the rear.
Bryer Court.entrance: Single entrance at the south (Ben Jonson House) end, via Fann Street ramp to north podium. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

listing.note: Single list entry for the whole Barbican complex (listed 5 Sep 2001); blocks are not separately listed.

Bunyan Court.name: Bunyan Court
Bunyan Court.named_after: John Bunyan (1628-1688), writer and Baptist preacher
Bunyan Court.story: Son of a Bedford tinker who became a tinker himself; never went to school but learnt to read and write at home.
Bunyan Court.types_note: Mainly two-storey maisonettes on a scissor plan around central corridors.
Bunyan Court.views: East-west block on the north podium forming the middle of a U with John Trundle Court and Bryer Court. North flats overlook Blake Tower; south flats overlook Beech Gardens.
Bunyan Court.features: Maisonettes with paired balconies on levels 2, 3 and 5; fitness centre beneath the podium; circular fountain pool.
Bunyan Court.entrance: Entrance and lift 59 at the Bryer Court end; built over the ramp from Fann Street. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

listing.note: Single list entry for the whole Barbican complex (listed 5 Sep 2001); blocks are not separately listed.

Cromwell Tower.name: Cromwell Tower
Cromwell Tower.story: Married Elizabeth Bourchier at St Giles Cripplegate in 1620 - the only link between Cromwell and the Barbican.
Cromwell Tower.types_note: Three large flats per floor, living rooms in the corners; penthouses of up to three storeys with roof gardens.
Cromwell Tower.views: Triangular tower at Beech Street and Silk Street. Flat 1s: east rooms, north balconies; 2s: north-east rooms, west balconies; 3s: west rooms, south balconies. Eastern-most tower.
Cromwell Tower.features: Upswept cantilevered balconies on every floor; jagged stepped top with penthouses and roof gardens; staffed foyer; 3 high-speed lifts; dramatic first-floor podium foyer. 123 m is the CTBUH architectural height.
Cromwell Tower.entrance: Main entrance at street level via Cromwell Place (Beech Street/Silk Street); podium entrance off Cromwell Highwalk. The tower is nearest to Moorgate. Station name for the entrance not stated.

Defoe House.name: Defoe House
Defoe House.named_after: Daniel Defoe (1660-1731), novelist, spy and journalist
Defoe House.story: Born Daniel Foe in the parish of St Giles Cripplegate; added the "De" himself. The block is pronounced De-FOE.
Defoe House.completed_note: December 1973; Phase II, Turriff then John Laing after disputes (known as Block IV).
Defoe House.types_note: Regular flats, 24 rooftop penthouses with barrel-vaulted roofs, and sub-podium garden flats (view over Thomas More Garden, no direct access).
Defoe House.views: Front-to-back block on the north side of Thomas More Garden. Living rooms face south over the garden/lake; bedrooms face north over Beech Gardens, Shakespeare Tower and Defoe Place.
Defoe House.features: Penthouses; garden flats; tenants stores; Defoe House/Shakespeare Tower car park (entrance off Beech Street).
Defoe House.entrance: Glazed entrances on Defoe Place at podium level for each of 12 staircases; staircase 1 opens at street level onto Lauderdale Place. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

listing.note: Single list entry for the whole Barbican complex (listed 5 Sep 2001); blocks are not separately listed.

Frobisher Crescent.name: Frobisher Crescent
Frobisher Crescent.named_after: Sir Martin Frobisher, Elizabethan seaman and privateer
Frobisher Crescent.story: Chosen to test Humphrey Gilbert's theory of a north-west passage; also held a privateering licence from Elizabeth I.
Frobisher Crescent.completed_note: Probably 1982 with the Barbican Centre (Barbican Living: no precise date); flats converted 2008-2010 (United House), 69 flats on levels 7-9.
Frobisher Crescent.types_note: Studios, 1, 2 and 3-bed apartments; top-floor flats have barrel-arched roofs with mezzanines; all have balconies, end flats wrap-around terraces.
Frobisher Crescent.views: Crescent north-west of the Barbican Centre, between Shakespeare Tower and the Centre; based on the old Jewin Crescent; straddles the north and south podia. Looks onto the "sculpture court" inside the crescent.
Frobisher Crescent.features: Designed as flats but turned into offices in the 1970s; fittings put in storage. Used by City University Business School, then converted: United House / TP Bennett, JCT D&B contract GBP 13.5m, Aug 2008-Jun 2010, flats sold by the City.
Frobisher Crescent.entrance: Part of the Barbican Centre complex; link to the Centre on the east side. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

listing.note: Single list entry for the whole Barbican complex (listed 5 Sep 2001); blocks are not separately listed.

Gilbert House.name: Gilbert House
Gilbert House.story: Lived in Redcross Street, whose route runs exactly under Gilbert House; Raleigh's half-brother and champion of the north-west passage.
Gilbert House.types_note: 1- to 5-room flats and penthouses; side-to-side with central corridor; no garden flats.
Gilbert House.views: Straddles the lake on tall stilts; Gilbert Bridge runs underneath. West flats look over the Barbican Centre terrace and lake; east flats look over the waterfall, towards Willoughby House.
Gilbert House.features: Built on stilts over the lake; pub (Crowders) under the south end of the bridge; foundation stone of the Arts Centre at the north end.
Gilbert House.entrance: Main entrance at podium level on Gilbert Bridge; lifts 50A/50B (south, near The Postern) and 52 (north). Nearest Tube not stated on source.

John Trundle Court.name: John Trundle Court
John Trundle Court.story: Published the "bad quarto" pirate Hamlet in 1603 with Nicholas Ling.
John Trundle Court.types_note: Studios (types F1A and F2A) and one-bedroom duplex penthouses (type P2A).
John Trundle Court.views: North-south block on the western edge of the estate along Aldersgate Street. West flats overlook Aldersgate Street and Barbican Tube station; east flats overlook Beech Gardens. Mirror image of Breton House.
John Trundle Court.features: Mezzanine entrances up tiled steps; rooftop glazed penthouses; Virgin Active gym partly under the block.
John Trundle Court.entrance: Via Fann Street ramp to the north podium or Beech Gardens/John Trundle Highwalk; lifts 55-58; lift 55 reaches Aldersgate Street near the bridge to Barbican Tube. Overlooks Barbican station.

Lambert Jones Mews.name: Lambert Jones Mews
Lambert Jones Mews.named_after: Richard Lambert Jones (1783-1863), Common Councilman for Cripplegate Without
Lambert Jones Mews.story: His 1824 motion to the Court of Common Council led to the founding of the Guildhall Library.
Lambert Jones Mews.completed_note: February 1974; Phase II, Turriff then John Laing.
Lambert Jones Mews.types_note: Two-storey mews houses, each with a garage; roof gardens.
Lambert Jones Mews.views: East-facing onto Thomas More Garden (many have back doors straight onto the garden); front doors onto a cobbled mews road below Lauderdale Place.
Lambert Jones Mews.features: Only homes with back doors straight onto a garden; roof gardens; garages.
Lambert Jones Mews.entrance: Front doors on the cobbled mews road below Lauderdale Place, entrance shared with Thomas More Car Park off Aldersgate Street. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

Lauderdale Tower.name: Lauderdale Tower
Lauderdale Tower.story: Built on the site of the London house of the Scottish earls of Lauderdale; first earl John Maitland was created in 1624.
Lauderdale Tower.completed_note: October 1974; Phase II, Turriff then John Laing.
Lauderdale Tower.types_note: Three large flats per floor in the corners; penthouse maisonettes.
Lauderdale Tower.views: Western-most tower, close to Barbican Tube and Aldersgate Street; overlooks Thomas More Garden. Flat 1s: west rooms/north balconies; 2s: north rooms/east balconies; 3s: east rooms/south balconies.
Lauderdale Tower.features: Upswept balconies; jagged penthouse tops with roof gardens; 3 high-speed lifts; staffed foyer. Featured in TV drama Luther.
Lauderdale Tower.entrance: Main entrance at street level via Lauderdale Place off Beech Street; podium entrance off the highwalk. Close to Barbican Tube station.

Mountjoy House.name: Mountjoy House
Mountjoy House.story: Shakespeare lodged with the Mountjoy family (Barbican Living: Monkwell Street, 1598-1612; City of London: Silver Street, 1604 - sources differ).
Mountjoy House.completed_note: April 1971; Phase II, Turriff then John Laing.
Mountjoy House.types_note: 2- to 5-room flats and penthouses, mostly identical to Gilbert House; side-to-side, central corridor, no garden flats.
Mountjoy House.views: North-south block joined to Thomas More House ("zig" to Seddon's "zag"), on tall columns above Mountjoy Close. East flats overlook St Giles Terrace, the small lake, the City Wall and Bastion; west flats overlook the City of London School for Girls grounds.
Mountjoy House.features: Unusually tall columns; ceremonial stairs to the lakeside (cut off); rooftop penthouses.
Mountjoy House.entrance: Lifts/stairs 25 (north, near Thomas More House) and 26 (south, shared with a public route). Nearest Tube not stated on source.

Seddon House.name: Seddon House
Seddon House.story: Converted London House, Aldersgate Street, into England's first big furniture store.
Seddon House.completed_note: May 1974; Phase II, Turriff then John Laing.
Seddon House.types_note: Studios to five-room penthouse maisonettes; side-to-side with central corridor.
Seddon House.views: Runs from Lauderdale Tower to Thomas More House on the west side of Thomas More Garden; rooms face west over the garden or east over Aldersgate Street.
Seddon House.features: Tall columns; rooftop penthouses (two bays wide); granite-faced lift lobbies at the north end.
Seddon House.entrance: Entrances at both ends; main entrance at podium level on Seddon Highwalk; 01 level is Lauderdale Place. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

Shakespeare Tower.name: Shakespeare Tower
Shakespeare Tower.story: Lodged with the Mountjoy family near the Barbican; the tower was long cited as Europe's highest residential building.
Shakespeare Tower.completed_note: February 1976; Phase Va, Sir Robert McAlpine - last building completed.
Shakespeare Tower.types_note: Three large flats per floor; penthouse maisonettes.
Shakespeare Tower.views: Centre tower, just west of the Barbican Centre; stands in the south podium, linked to the north podium. Flat 1s: south rooms/east balconies; 2s: east rooms/north balconies; 3s: north rooms/west balconies.
Shakespeare Tower.features: Upswept balconies; penthouses with roof gardens; Guinness Book of Records highest residential building in Europe for many years.
Shakespeare Tower.entrance: Main entrance from Defoe Place at south podium level; second entrance off Beech Garden on the north podium. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

Speed House.name: Speed House
Speed House.story: Probably born in St Paul's churchyard; freed from the family tailoring trade by Sir Fulk Greville's patronage to pursue maps.
Speed House.completed_note: July 1969; first Barbican block built; Phase III, John Laing (Block VI).
Speed House.types_note: Regular flats; penthouses; two-storey garden maisonettes below podium (mainly Type 84).
Speed House.views: Front-to-back block in the north-east corner; forms the northern edge of Speed Gardens; living rooms look south over the garden and lake (sub-podium flats south only).
Speed House.features: Garden maisonettes with car ports; penthouses with barrel vaults; Speed Garden playground.
Speed House.entrance: Doors at podium level on Speed Highwalk; street-level access from Silk Street beside the Guildhall School. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

Thomas More House.name: Thomas More House
Thomas More House.named_after: Sir Thomas More (1478-1535), lawyer, statesman and saint
Thomas More House.story: Born in Milk Street; "the King's good servant, but God's first".
Thomas More House.completed_note: September 1973; Phase II, Turriff then John Laing (Block XI).
Thomas More House.types_note: Regular flats; penthouses; three storeys of garden flats below podium (lowest studios, two upper levels larger).
Thomas More House.views: Front-to-back block along Thomas More Garden, the largest of the Barbican gardens. Above-podium living rooms face south over the City of London School for Girls tennis courts; north view over the garden. Garden flats face the garden.
Thomas More House.features: Garden flats facing the largest garden; penthouses; Thomas More Car Park at 03 level.
Thomas More House.entrance: Glazed doors at podium level on Thomas More Highwalk; gates onto Thomas More Garden; 03-level entrance on the cobbled road to the car park. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

listing.note: Single list entry for the whole Barbican complex (listed 5 Sep 2001); blocks are not separately listed.

Willoughby House.name: Willoughby House
Willoughby House.story: Married Charles Brandon, owner of the Barbican manor, in 1533; the name revives the old Willoughby House that stood here.
Willoughby House.types_note: Mostly "up and over" scissor maisonettes plus penthouse maisonettes; flats are rarely identical.
Willoughby House.views: Eastern edge of the estate, runs from Speed House to Andrewes House. Living rooms face west over the lake (past Brandon Mews domes); bedrooms face east over Moor Lane / Britannic Tower.
Willoughby House.features: Up-and-over maisonettes; the estate's eastern edge; planted Willoughby Highwalk.
Willoughby House.entrance: Main entrances on Willoughby Highwalk; lifts at both ends and centre. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

listing.note: Single list entry for the whole Barbican complex (listed 5 Sep 2001); blocks are not separately listed.

Brandon Mews.name: Brandon Mews
Brandon Mews.named_after: The Brandon family, lords of the manor of Barbican
Brandon Mews.story: Charles Brandon, Duke of Suffolk, held the manor of Base Court (Barbican); earlier Robert Brandon (d.1369), son of Lord Ufford, acquired it.
Brandon Mews.types_note: Two-storey mews houses with internal bathrooms and angled roof lights; brown perspex roof canopy added in the 1980s.
Brandon Mews.views: West-facing; views over the lake behind the waterfall or over Speed Garden (no direct access).
Brandon Mews.features: Roof canopy of brown perspex (1980s); water chute / waterfall into the lake.
Brandon Mews.entrance: Entrances down from podium on Willoughby Highwalk, each serving two houses; parking by the rear doors. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

The Postern.name: The Postern
The Postern.named_after: The postern: a back door or side gate, here referring to the posterns in the City Wall at Cripplegate
The Postern.story: Barbican Living defines a postern via the OED as a back door or side gate, in the context of the City Wall gates of Cripplegate ward.
The Postern.completed_note: March 1971; Phase II, Turriff then John Laing.
The Postern.types_note: Long narrow town houses with garages, open-tread dog-leg stairs, roof gardens.
The Postern.views: Overlook St Giles Church and the lake extension between the church and the City Wall.
The Postern.features: Glazed engineering brick cladding; link between Gilbert Bridge and Wallside.
The Postern.entrance: Front doors on the covered Postern Bridge towards London Wall; stairs down to St Giles Terrace. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

listing.note: Single list entry for the whole Barbican complex (listed 5 Sep 2001); blocks are not separately listed.

Wallside.name: Wallside
Wallside.named_after: The Roman / City Wall beside it
Wallside.story: Runs parallel to surviving remains of the Roman wall.
Wallside.completed_note: March 1971; Phase II, Turriff then John Laing.
Wallside.types_note: Town houses with integral garages and roof terraces; entered at podium level.
Wallside.views: The only part of the estate where homes face outward; front overlooks Bridgewater Square, back overlooks St Giles Terrace, the lake and the City Wall.
Wallside.features: Roof terraces; Roman wall views; glazed engineering brick.
Wallside.entrance: Street doors on the square; upper entrances from the highwalk. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

Milton Court.name: Milton Court
Milton Court.story: Replaced the demolished Milton Court (a fire station, medical facilities and flats). Not part of the Grade II listing.
Milton Court.views: Corner of Silk Street and Moor Lane, next to the Guildhall School.
Milton Court.features: Guildhall School annexe in the lower six floors; eight-storey atrium.
Milton Court.entrance: Close to Barbican and Moorgate Tube stations (Wikipedia).

Blake Tower.name: Blake Tower
Blake Tower.category: adjacent - not part of the estate proper
Blake Tower.story: Named for the poet and painter; no namesake story on the sources fetched.
Blake Tower.completed_note: Built 1965-71 as the Barbican YMCA (Phase IV, Myton); converted 2015-16 by Redrow Homes for the City. Note: brief said 2017 - sources found say 2015-16.
Blake Tower.types_note: Studios to 3-bed; mostly 1- and 2-bed; two duplexes on floors 16-17.
Blake Tower.views: On Fann Street beside the ramp from Goswell Road; links the Barbican to the Golden Lane Estate (height echoes Great Arthur House).
Blake Tower.features: Exotic projecting concrete fire-escape stairs; design echoes Golden Lane tower height. Barbican Living treats it as an estate block; it is owned by the City and covered by the same 2001 list entry (as "YMCA"), though physically separate.
Blake Tower.entrance: 2 Fann Street, EC2Y 8BR, by the Goswell Road ramp. Nearest Tube not stated on source.

Golden Lane Estate.name: Golden Lane Estate
Golden Lane Estate.story: Chamberlin, Powell and Bon's first big commission, won in the 1951-52 competition; built 1953-62 for City workers as council housing; the Barbican followed on the south side.
Golden Lane Estate.features: Great Arthur House was briefly London's tallest residential building and the first to break the 100 ft limit; Crescent House Grade II*.

The stairs go down to a lower level where there is first a separate WC and then a bathroom. Then there are two bedrooms. There are six Type 51 flats in Defoe House. The flat runs from front to back of the building and so it is only found on the top floors of the north-south-facing terraces fronting the lake. Type 60 is a variant on the Type 23 layout. But where the Type 23 is a simple rectangular-shaped unit, the Type 60 has an extra alcove in one bedroom wall – big enough for a fitted wardrobe. 61.layout: Type 61 is a two-bedroom penthouse flat. There are two: both in Defoe House, and they come at either end of Defoe House, where the extra wall of windows gives scope for more rooms. The living room takes the central position with the windows looking east towards Smithfield or west towards the Barbican Centre and lakeside terrace. There is a bedroom at either side. The single Type 86 penthouse in Speed House is very similar. Click here for more detailed information on ‘Two bedroom flats’.

63/64.layout: Types 63/64 are the layouts of all 14 of the houses in Wallside. They have 4 bedrooms, a living room, a dining room (6 rooms), 2 bathrooms, a cloakroom, a roof terrace, an integral garage, and a store. I have no idea why it’s ’63/64′ – there’s only the one design layout shown in the original Barbican letting brochure.

67/68.layout: Types 67/68 are the layouts of all seven of the houses in The Postern. They have 4 bedrooms, a living room, a dining room (6 rooms), 2 bathrooms, a roof terrace, an integral garage, and a store. I have no idea why it’s ’67/68′ – there’s only the one design layout shown in the original Barbican letting brochures.

6B.layout: Unfortunately, I don’t have a plan for Type 6B. This Barbican flat type wasn’t shown in the original brochures for Barbican tower flats. But I know from lists produced by the City when the Barbican estate was built that the Type 6B flat has 2 bedrooms, a living room, a dining area (4 rooms) a bathroom and a shower room. There’s only one Type 6B flat and it is in Lauderdale Tower. It has rooms along the north-facing side of the tower, and balconies looking east. Click here for much more detailed information about tower flats .

70.layout: Type 70 is a one-bedroom flat. At the Barbican Centre end of Gilbert House, there are two end flats on each of the six floors (making 12 flats in all). These are Type 70s. Type 70 flats are squeezed into a slightly unusual shape by the larger than usual space for the entrance, stairs and lift unit. There is a dining area in front of the kitchen, as with the normal flats, and a living room (albeit a shallow one), then a dressing room, then a bedroom at the far end with windows in two walls. Click here for more detailed information on ‘One bedroom flats’.

71.layout: Type 71 is a one-bedroom flat, which only appears in Gilbert House. There is one Type 71 flat on each of the six floors of Gilbert House – as a counterpart to Type 39 and Type 41 flats. Together they make up the flats at the Andrewes House end of the terrace. The Type 71 flats are smaller than the Type 39s and Type 41s because space is given up to the connecting section to the adjoining Andrewes House corridors. The Type 71 flats have a living area and a bedroom. Click here for more detailed information on ‘One bedroom flats’.

72.layout: Type 72 is a one-bedroom penthouse flat. At the Barbican Centre end of Gilbert House, there are two end penthouse flats on the top floor. These are Type 72s. The Type 72 penthouses are squeezed into a slightly unusual shape by the larger than usual space for the entrance, stairs and lift unit. There is only space for a living area and a bedroom. There is also a roof patio for each flat. Click here for more detailed information on ‘Penthouses’ . Click here for more detailed information on ‘One-bedroom flats’ .

73.layout: Type 73 is a studio penthouse flat. Type 73 is the layout of the penthouse flat on the corner of Gilbert House where it joins Andrewes House. There was only space for one studio room. Click here for more detailed information on ‘Studio flats’.

74.layout: Type 74 is a one-bedroom flat. Type 74 is the layout of the penthouse flat on the corner of Gilbert House, directly overlooking to St Giles’ Church. So it has quite a view. Type 74 closely resembles Type 46 , the layout of a similar penthouse flat on the top floor of Seddon House. Type 74 follows an unusual ‘S’ shape, presumably using up left-over space. Many Barbican flats are ‘L’ shaped – this living room is more like ‘V’ shaped round the kitchen, with a bedroom at the other end. Click here for more detailed information on ‘One bedroom flats’.

76.layout: Type 76 is a one-bedroom flat . Type 76 is the standard layout of lakeside flats in Andrewes House. There are 14 in all with their distinctive windows shaped like a ‘U’, looking out onto the igloos in the lake and the waterfall. The living room is at lakeside and there is one bedroom at the back, facing Fore Street. Type 76 flats are almost identical to the upper garden level Type 16 flats, which form an upper (but still sub-Podium) floor above, except that the Type 16 flats are all on one level, whereas the lakeside Type 76s have steps down to the living area. 79.layout: Type 79 is a one-bedroom flat. Type 79 is the layout of garden and upper garden level flats in Andrewes House, at the corner with Brandon Mews. They face only onto Fore Street. At the opposite side of the living room, there is a door into ‘dressing room’ (which is what architects call spaces without windows they couldn’t think of an obvious use for. 81.layout: There is only one Type 81 flat and it is in Andrewes House. It is the flat which originally went with the pub (now a restaurant). The flat has a large living room and two bedrooms apparently. I don’t have a plan. Click here for more detailed information on ‘Two bedroom flats’.

The only comparable flats elsewhere are the Type 51 maisonettes in Defoe House. Click here for more detailed information on ‘Maisonettes’.

Each of these flats has a living area and one bedroom at the front over the garden, a largish reception or study opposite the main door in the middle of the flat, and a second bedroom and a dining area at the back. It’s markedly wider – by a room size – than the Defoe Type 57 . Speed House is very like Defoe House above Podium level. 9A.layout: Type 9A is a Barbican flat type on the 10th, 20th and 30th floors in Shakespeare Tower. Types 9A, 9B and 9C are variants on the standard 8A , 8B and 8C models to take account of communal water tanks which are needed every ten floors in the Barbican towers. Type 9A has 3 bedrooms, a living room, a breakfast room (4/5 rooms) a kitchen and a bathroom. It is the standard Type 8A layout, but without the shower room. Type 9A flats have rooms along the south-facing side of Shakespeare Tower, and balconies looking east. Click here for much more detailed information about tower flats .

F1A.layout: The Type F1A flat must be about the most compact home on the estate. It’s a small ‘studio’ flat with a kitchen, a bathroom, and a room to live and sleep in at the window end. The entrance is off a central spiral stairwell and lift unit. This ‘core’ takes up one third of the depth of the building, leaving room for an F1A at the front and one at the back. There are 33 such flats in Breton House and 38 in John Trundle Court. They are usually found in a four-flat combination consisting of two Type F1A flats and two Type F2A flats. timeline.event: Roman fort built at Cripplegate (90-120 AD); city wall built around c. 200 AD incorporates it. 'Barbican' derives from Low Latin barbecana, an outer fortification or gateway.
Medieval Jewish cemetery on the site expanded (1268-1290); Jews expelled 1290; site granted to William de Montford 12 Jul 1291. Excavated before construction (reported 1961).
Population of the Cripplegate parish c. 14,000 in the 1850s; by 1951 the resident population of the whole City was 5,324, of whom 48 lived in Cripplegate.
Air raid (Blitz) destroys most of Cripplegate. Historic England and ArchDaily give 29 Dec 1940.
timeline.note: Disputed detail: Londonist says Cripplegate was first hit on 25 Aug 1940 and suffered through the war; 29 Dec is the big fire raid date used by Historic England.

timeline.event: Town and Country Planning Act 1947 lets authorities such as the City Corporation buy large areas for redevelopment, making the Barbican project possible.

Golden Lane Estate competition (City Corporation). Powell, Chamberlin and Bon, all teaching at Kingston, each submit a scheme under a pact to partner if any won. Powell wins. (Guardian and AJ: three schemes submitted; AJ credits the win to 1951/1952.)
Chamberlin, Powell and Bon practice founded. City discussions on the future of the bombed Barbican site begin in 1952.

CPB report to the City: the site can hold a viable community of about 7,000 people. Dec 1955: Special Committee instructs CPB to prepare a scheme for the non-commercial part. (Earlier a commercial 'Martin-Mealand' scheme was also on the table; a faction wanted business use.)
CPB 1956 report with large-scale model; proposes five towers (three survive into final plan).
Court of Common Council accepts as policy that the site be a residential area, aimed at middle and higher income groups.
CPB engaged on limited terms (40,000 guineas to prospectus, up to 40,000 more if retained). Not yet committed as architects for construction.

London County Council grants outline planning permission with conditions: density cut from 300 to 230 persons per acre, 1.5 acres open space per 1,000 residents, railway cutting to be covered, car parking provided. North Barbican rezoned from commercial to residential.
CPB's seminal 1959 'Barbican Redevelopment' report (the scheme that was approved to go ahead; Arup consulted on structure).
Barbican Committee puts the 1959 report to the Court of Common Council; City (not private developers) to carry out the development.
Historic England: construction was conceived in the 1940s but did not start until 1960, when CPB moved from recommending to overseeing the scheme.
timeline.note: Start dates conflict across sources: 1960 (HE), 1962 (listing, Westminster, Barbican Living Phase I), 1963 (City 2019 press), 1965 (City history page; Wikipedia). Phase I contract was let April 1962.

timeline.event: Phase I (Milton Court public services building) contract won by J Jarvis & Sons at GBP 467,250; site had earlier been cleared of 150,000+ cubic yards of ruins.

Railway between Barbican and Moorgate realigned underground. Widened Lines tunnel opened 21 Jun 1965; Metropolitan/Circle services moved into new tunnels 6 Dec 1965 (one source). Wikipedia: 500 m realigned 1963-65.
John Laing signs Phase III (east: Speed, Gilbert, Andrewes, Brandon Mews, Willoughby, Cromwell Tower) for just under GBP 6m; final cost over GBP 11.5m.
City asks CPB for an expanded theatre and concert hall; the arts centre is shoe-horned into the plan after building has begun. Final theatre design April 1968.
Phase IV (north Barbican) awarded to Myton (Taylor Woodrow) for GBP 5,581,022; later a 14-month strike/lock-out.

First tenants move in; estate officially opened July 1969 (City 2019 press release says first tenants in Andrewes House). Barbican Living records Speed House completed Jul 1969, Gilbert Aug, Andrewes Nov 1969.
timeline.note: Which block was first occupied: Andrewes House (City press office) vs Speed House (Wikipedia/Barbican Living completion sequence). Treat as unresolved.

timeline.event: Barbican Centre construction begins (built 1971-82; arts centre largely designed in its present form 1968). The Postern and Wallside completed Mar 1971, Mountjoy Apr 1971, Willoughby House Apr 1971.
North Barbican blocks complete: John Trundle Court Oct 1972, Breton House Nov, Bunyan Court Dec; Bryer Court Feb 1973, Ben Jonson House Mar 1973.
Cromwell Tower completed.
Thomas More House Sep 1973; Defoe House Dec 1973.
Lambert Jones Mews Feb 1974; Seddon House May 1974; Lauderdale Tower Oct 1974.
Responsibility for residential management passes to a new Barbican Management Committee; renamed Barbican Residential Committee 19 May 1978.
timeline.note: Two dates for committee creation on Barbican Living: 6 Jan 1975 vs 1 Apr 1975.

timeline.event: Shakespeare Tower (Phase Va, built by Sir Robert McAlpine) completed; last residential block.
Housing Act 1980 in force; City Corporation counts as local authority so Right to Buy applies to Barbican flats.
Start date of the 125-year term of most Barbican long leases (exceptions: Cromwell Tower 16 Jun 1982; Lambert Jones Mews 6 Jun 1985; Mountjoy House 25 Feb 1982; The Postern 16 Sep 1982).

Queen opens Barbican Centre; calls it 'one of the wonders of the modern world'. 3,500 at opening night, LSO and RSC perform, fireworks over the lake. Cost quoted GBP 153m (BBC), GBP 159m (Barbican Living) or GBP 161m (Wikipedia). Public opening 4 Mar.
Queen Mother plants a mulberry tree near the children's playground in Thomas More Garden.
Canopy roof with steel frame and polycarbonate vaults put over Brandon Mews to stop leaks.
Property Week: about 18 years after tenants began to buy, all but about 300 of c. 2,000 flats are owner-occupied.
Barbican complex listed Grade II (Minister for the Arts Tessa Blackstone's announcement; listing reference 1352667). (Wikipedia: listing covers the whole complex except the former Milton Court.)
Estate landscape added to the Register of Parks and Gardens at Grade II*.
Residents' referendum on taking over management of the estate is heavily defeated; Residents Consultation Committee formed 2003.
City Corporation adopts the Barbican Listed Building Management Guidelines (prepared with Avanti Architects, English Heritage, resident reps and the Twentieth Century Society).
Top floors of Frobisher Crescent converted to flats (2009 per Barbican Living, 2010 per Conservation Area SPD). Milton Court demolished 2010 (Barbican Living), replaced by The Heron.
timeline.note: Milton Court demolition year varies: 2008 in Wikipedia CPB article, 2010 in Barbican Living.

timeline.event: Former YMCA hostel converted by Redrow to 74 flats (Blake Tower), run as part of the estate. SPD says works 2013-17.
Barbican and Golden Lane Conservation Area designated (estate had previously not been in a conservation area).
50th anniversary of first residents (July).
Allies and Morrison with Asif Khan Studio chosen to lead Barbican Centre renewal; construction budget GBP 50-150m at that time.
Public consultation on Lakeside, foyers and Conservatory renewal.
City Corporation approves planning application for Barbican Renewal Phase 1 (City commits GBP 191m of GBP 231m). Major on-site works from 2027; most Centre activities pause Jun 2028-29.

people.name: Peter 'Joe' Chamberlin
people.role: Dominant force in the partnership on the Barbican; architect in charge of the theatre until succeeded by Bon. CBE 1974, ARA 1975, RA 1978 (two weeks before he died). Conscientious objector in WWII; qualified at Kingston 1948. Died before the estate was complete.

people.name: Geoffry Powell
people.role: Won the 1951 Golden Lane competition. Born in India (Anglo-Indian military family). Said of the Barbican 'in the end it killed our practice'. Retired 1985.

people.name: Christoph Bon
people.role: Swiss, born St Gallen, ETH Zurich; worked in Milan 1946-49 then taught at Kingston. Partner in charge of the arts centre and Guildhall School with Chamberlin (listing text); took over the theatre.
people.note: AJ obituary says 'aged 88', Guardian says 78; birth year 1921 implies 78.

people.name: Chamberlin, Powell and Bon
people.role: Practice formed after the Golden Lane win. The Barbican office employed 70+ people with a separate office for the job. Wound up in 1987 (merged with Austin-Smith:Lord).

people.name: John Honer and Gordon Ruwald
people.role: Project architects on the Arts Centre; John Honer executive architect on the Guildhall School.

people.name: Ove Arup and Partners
people.role: Structural engineers. Advised in the 1959 report on foundations on London clay, vibration isolation of the railway (acoustic consultants Dr P. Grootenhuis and Dr Parfitt, Building Research Station), and later the arts-centre substructure (about 190,000 cubic metres of excavation, 1974 jacking of cables near the towers).

people.name: Herbert Spencer
people.role: Designed the typeface and signage around the estate; the little castle motif depicts the Roman watchtower ('barbican').

people.name: Richard Southern
people.role: Theatre consultant to the 1959 theatre scheme.

people.name: City of London Corporation
people.role: Client, landlord and developer. Court of Common Council decided 19 Sep 1957 to build housing; the Barbican Committee ran the build; the Barbican Residential Committee (from 1975/78) manages the estate. The Corporation funded the arts centre as 'the City's gift to the nation'.

people.name: Contractors
people.role: Phase I Jarvis; Phase II Turriff then John Laing; Phase III and V John Laing; Phase IV Myton (Taylor Woodrow); Phase Va (Shakespeare Tower) Sir Robert McAlpine. Mowlem cleared and piled the Phase IV site; Higgs and Hill built the new rail tunnels (one source).

design.summary: Flats: 2,014 per Wikipedia and the LSO; City of London web page says 'over 2,060' (the later count likely includes Blake Tower and Frobisher Crescent conversions; this is my inference, not a source statement). Residents: 'around 4,000' / 'more than 4,000'. Planned population in 1955 was about 7,000. 140 flat types (City press 2019) vs over 100 (Historic England). Site: 35 acres / 14 ha (Wikipedia, Allies and Morrison) vs 40 acres (City). Estate: 4 tower blocks (incl. Blake Tower), 14 terrace blocks, 2 mews (Wikipedia).

Raised pedestrian level 1 to 3 storeys above ground; roads and car parks below. Terrace blocks rise up to seven floors above the podium. The scheme followed the post-war ideal of separating pedestrians from vehicles (the Police Commissioner pushed for even more segregation in 1959). The elevated walkway system was designed to be part of a wider City plan. Navigation is notoriously hard; yellow lines guide visitors.

Three towers: Cromwell (completed Jan 1973), Lauderdale (Oct 1974), Shakespeare (Feb 1976). Height 123 m / 404 ft (Skyscraper Center); the City's 2019 press release says 126 m (404 ft), which is inconsistent in itself. Floor counts vary by method: 42 (Skyscraper Center, Wikipedia); 43 (Cromwell) and 44 (Lauderdale, Shakespeare) above podium including garage and foyer levels (Barbican Living). Each floor has three flats, one per side of the triangle; top 2-3 floors are penthouses. Lauderdale: 114 flats plus 3 penthouse maisonettes. Early plans: 1956 five towers (30 storeys); 1959 37-storey polygonal; decision for 43/44 storeys made 1961. Claims: 'tallest residential towers in Europe' at the time (City guide; Guinness per Barbican Living); in London until surpassed by Pan Peninsula (Wikipedia). ArchDaily says original plans were five towers of twenty storeys, which conflicts with Barbican Living (30 storeys).

Poured in situ reinforced concrete; exposed surfaces mostly pick-hammered with smaller areas bush-hammered, exposing Pen Lee granite aggregate (listing text). Done by hand tools after the shutters were struck, only once concrete had cured at least 28 days, progressively as the building rose. Contractor recollections (Westminster oral-history pamphlet) say the work was dirty, dusty and labour intensive, with white-finger vibration problems, and was done by a small group of black workers using Kango hammers ('probably about half a dozen coloured guys' in one recollection). That is an oral-history account from one site, not a documented labour census. The City calls the finish 'expensive and time-consuming', a sign of its commitment to quality.

Stretches of London Wall survive in the estate (scheduled monument). The wall as seen is largely medieval/Tudor brick on Roman foundations. A stretch at St Alphage Garden keeps brick crenellations thought to date from the Wars of the Roses. St Giles Cripplegate (Grade I) stands at the centre of the estate. Archaeology on the Jewish cemetery done before construction.

Lakes and landscaped gardens designed to give an aspect to every flat; brick-surfaced walkways and planters keep a minimal material palette. Landscape is on the Register of Parks and Gardens at Grade II* (Feb 2003). Lakes refurbished in 2004; Beech Gardens relined 2012. Open space required by LCC: 1.5 acres per 1,000 residents.

Tropical conservatory on top of the arts-centre fly tower; the idea came partly from the need to screen the 'uglier shape' of the theatre fly tower. Now about 1,500 species of plants and trees, with fish and terrapin ponds. Renewal plans reuse conservatory glass.

Sliding timber windows with metal and glass balustrades (Historic England listing quote on the towers); ArchDaily says windows pivot horizontally for cleaning from inside (check against the sliding description before using either). Balconies are on bedrooms and studies too, not just living rooms. Tower balconies are upswept and wrap round. Towers have lifts with small panel doors from lift to a service cupboard so milk and post can be delivered without leaving the lift (ArchDaily quoting a period source). Kitchens: fitted, with built-in Creda fridge, dishwasher, eye-level cooker, extractor and stainless sink with waste disposal.

Sink-mounted Garchey unit: a plug in the sink drops wet waste (and cans/bottles) into a bulb under the sink; flushing sends it down cast-iron pipes to 150 pits and 2 miles of tunnels to two control centres (under Defoe House and Andrewes House), where tanker vacuum lorries empty them. Rainwater from roofs shares the system. Early staff: 15 handling 24 tonnes a week; later 3 staff and 2 tons every three weeks. 600 units were removed by 2004 leaving over 1,400. Original manufacturer Matthew Hall Ltd. Invented by Frenchman Louis Garchey; first UK use Leeds 1935.

Electric cables embedded in the floor screed over an insulating quilt, chosen over oil-fired central heating in the 1959 report; background warmth plus individual electric fires; cheap off-peak tariff; occupants cannot switch the background heat off. Under leases the background heating runs 1 Oct to 30 Apr. Note: Wikipedia mentions a 'Citigen' district heating system for the centre; I did not verify that for the flats.

Four railway tracks ran in an open cutting through the site. A new tunnel was built like a bowstring between Moorgate and Barbican, then the old route was absorbed. Tunnel is 305 m long, box-in-box on rubber bearings (one source calls it the world's first floating slab track; unverified). Foundations: under-reamed bored piles 915-1220 mm diameter up to 18 m deep into London clay, loads up to 1,800 tons; towers on cylinder caissons. Arts centre excavation about 190,000 m3.

Industrial disputes ran through the 1960s and 70s: Turriff left Phase II; Myton had a 14-month strike. Barbican Centre budget about GBP 14m for the construction contract grew to GBP 159m total by 1982 (Barbican Living, a 'more than tenfold' increase).

design.topic: Tenure: leasehold and Right to Buy
design.summary: Built as rental housing for City professionals at market rents, owned by the Corporation (a local authority under the Housing Act 1980), so Right to Buy applied from 3 Oct 1980. Buyers got a long lease: most leases are 125 years from 1 Jul 1981 (a few blocks later). Extension rights of 90 years under the 1993 Act after two years' ownership. In 1999 all but about 300 of c. 2,000 flats were owner-occupied. A few remain let by the City. Note: one academic article puts the change at 1982; the Act commenced Oct 1980 and lease terms run from 1981.

Barbican complex listed Grade II on 5 Sep 2001 (as a whole, ref. 1352667), landscape Grade II* on the Register (Feb 2003), London Wall scheduled monument, St Giles Grade I, Barbican and Golden Lane Conservation Area designated Oct 2018. Listed Building Management Guidelines adopted 24 May 2005 and later adopted as SPDs; most alterations need listed building consent.

facts.fact: By 1951 only 48 people lived in the whole of Cripplegate ward, out of 5,324 in the City.
The three architects each entered the Golden Lane competition separately; the pact was that whoever won would partner with the other two. Powell won. The practice was in business a year later.
The brutalist estate was designed so that flats in towers could take milk and post through the lift: each lift has a small door to a service cupboard.
A Garchey sink unit let residents dump wet rubbish and tins into the sink; the estate has about 2 miles of tunnel and 150 pits under it for the waste.

The Barbican sits on the medieval Jewish cemetery (the Jewin Street / 'Jew's Garden' area), the only permitted Jewish burial ground in England until 1177 according to Look Up London; Museum of London excavation papers were published in 1961.
The 'Mendelssohn tree' on the highwalk is the stump of a 500-year-old Burnham Beeches beech that fell in January 1990. Burnham Beeches is owned by the City. The Mendelssohn story is rumour.
Queen Mother planted a mulberry in Thomas More Garden in 1984; no one knows how she got in without a resident's key.
The terrapins in the Conservatory ponds were reportedly moved from Hampstead Heath ponds after terrorising local wildlife (Londonist's wording, anecdotal).
The 1975 Disney film One of Our Dinosaurs Is Missing shows the Barbican towers in a scene set in the 1920s; Gangster No. 1 (set from 1968) shows Shakespeare Tower, which opened 1976.
The little castle motif seen around the estate depicts the Roman watchtower (barbican) and was the original estate logo; Herbert Spencer designed the signage and typeface.
Barbican staff report ghostly Roman centurions on Level -2 where the Roman fort stood (staff anecdote on the Barbican's own page, not verified).
Barbican Centre opening night 3 Mar 1982: 3,500 guests, fireworks over the lake, broadcast on BBC2 in full; public opened next day.
The Barbican Centre cost grew from about GBP 14m contract price to about GBP 159m by 1982.
The gold refiner's frieze from 53-54 Barbican survived the Blitz, was demolished 1962 but the frieze was kept and now stands at a western entrance to the estate.
J.G. Ballard's High-Rise is said to be inspired largely by the Barbican towers; Star Wars TV series Andor used the estate as Coruscant backdrop; Quantum of Solace used it as MI6.
The estate has its own door-numbering and yellow guide lines because visitors and delivery drivers could not find their way (anecdotal travel-site source).
A promotional film for Unit 4 + 2's 'Concrete and Clay' was shot on the Barbican building site in 1965.
Residents voted in May 2003 on taking over management of the estate and rejected it heavily.
